exam: What investigations would you order for a 6‑month‑old with failure to thrive and recurrent oral thrush? — PCR for HIV, CD4 count, full blood count, and chest X‑ray if respiratory symptoms; explain why each is needed.

A child on first‑line ART presents with severe diarrhoea and weight loss. How do you differentiate HIV progression from a new opportunistic infection? — Review viral load, CD4 trend, stool microscopy, and consider TB or cryptosporidiosis; management differs.
Explain why nevirapine is avoided as a first‑line drug in children with high baseline viral load. — High resistance risk; newer integrase inhibitors have better efficacy and safety.
How would you manage a child with suspected PCP when oxygen and bronchoscopy are unavailable? — Start high‑dose cotrimoxazole empirically, give supplemental oxygen if possible, monitor response.
Describe the WHO clinical staging criteria that would place a child in Stage 3. — Chronic diarrhoea, severe weight loss, recurrent severe bacterial infections, or persistent fever.
What red‑flag symptom in a paediatric HIV patient mandates immediate referral? — Acute respiratory distress or severe dehydration; requires urgent higher‑level care.

How does PMTCT reduce vertical transmission, and what are the key components in low‑resource settings? — Maternal ART during pregnancy, intrapartum prophylaxis, and infant nevirapine for 6 weeks; simple, cost‑effective regimens.

Differentiate between HIV‑related lymphadenopathy and tuberculous lymphadenitis on exam. — HIV nodes are usually generalized, non‑tender; TB nodes are often unilateral, matted, and may have sinus formation.
ai.title: HIV Infection in Children
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Overview of paediatric HIV as presented in the UNAIDS 2022 fact sheet, focusing on diagnosis, staging, common co‑morbidities in low‑resource settings, and practical management for East African hospitals.

b: Confirmed by a positive HIV DNA PCR (or viral load) after 4 weeks of age.
Rapid antibody test is unreliable before 18 months; use PCR instead.
sections.p: HIV infection in children is the presence of HIV‑1 or HIV‑2 virus acquired perinatally, through breastfeeding, or via blood exposure.

b: Stage 1: Asymptomatic or mild lymphadenopathy.
Stage 2: Moderate weight loss, recurrent oral thrush.
Stage 3: Severe weight loss, chronic diarrhoea, severe bacterial infections.
Stage 4: Opportunistic infections (e.g., PCP, CMV retinitis) or HIV‑related malignancy.
sections.p: WHO clinical staging (2021) is used where CD4 counts are unavailable; otherwise WHO immunological categories apply.

b: Maternal HIV with no antiretroviral prophylaxis.
Breastfeeding from an untreated mother.
Blood transfusion with unscreened products (rare).
sections.p: In East Africa the dominant route is vertical transmission.

b: Failure to thrive (weight/height <‑2 SD).
Chronic diarrhoea >2 weeks.
Recurrent oral or skin candidiasis.
Persistent fever without source.
sections.p: Children may be asymptomatic early, then develop growth failure, recurrent infections, or developmental delay.

sections.p: Identify life‑threatening opportunistic infections and organ failure early.

Avoid nevirapine in children with high baseline viral load due to resistance risk.
Treat opportunistic infections: cotrimoxazole prophylaxis, fluconazole for thrush, TMP‑SMX for PCP.
Nutritional rehabilitation and micronutrient supplementation.
sections.p: Start antiretroviral therapy (ART) promptly, treat co‑infections, and provide supportive care.

Growth chart at each visit.

sections.p: Regular monitoring of growth, viral load, and CD4; reinforce prevention of mother‑to‑child transmission (PMTCT).
